_readme: The game over. Four bars at 120, which is eight seconds - the same length as the
overworld theme, because a screen you sit on deciding what to do about a lost run is
the one place a short loop nags hardest.
IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE CODE IT REPLACED WAS WRONG ABOUT THE GENRE. _on_battle_finished
cut the music dead at a defeat and justified it in a comment: 'every game this borrows
from cuts the music at a game over'. Final Fantasy I ships 'Dead Music' in 1987, and
each Final Fantasy since has had its own game-over scene. The references CHANGE what
is playing at a death; they do not fall silent. See docs/GENRE_CONVENTIONS.md 14.
Slow WITHOUT a slow tempo: the grid is the same 120 every other tune here uses, and the
weight comes from note LENGTH - halves and wholes where the fight moves in eighths. One
bpm across the soundtrack means the three voices render at one grid and a reader
comparing two files is comparing the music rather than the arithmetic.
A minor: Am - F - Dm - E, the oldest lament progression there is, ending on the
dominant so the loop's return to A is the resolution. The same last-bar constraint
skirmish is written under, for the same reason - Tune.render writes no fade tail.
NO DRUM. A death with a beat under it is a march, and this is a stand-still. The third
voice is a bell an octave up answering the lead on the half bar, which is the one thing
that keeps eight seconds of long notes from reading as a held chord.
